source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Blind expert review found LLM-agent ideas rated more novel than ideas written by expert NLP researchers.
numbers: Novelty mean 4.84 human vs 5.64 AI vs 5.81 AI+rerank (1-10). Per-review N: human 119, AI 109, AI+rerank 109; p<0.01 both. Per-idea (N=49 per arm): 4.86 vs 5.62 (p=0.03) vs 5.78 (p<0.01). 79 reviewers, 298 reviews.
limits: Novelty judged at idea stage only; Welch t-tests with Bonferroni; one domain (NLP prompting topics).
agent_relevance: A generator can beat experts on rated novelty. Rated novelty is not proof of breakthrough value (see c05).

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Novelty gain came with no gain in feasibility or expected effectiveness; overall score only rose with reranking.
numbers: Feasibility 6.61 human vs 6.34 AI vs 6.44 rerank (n.s.). Effectiveness 5.13 vs 5.47 vs 5.55 (n.s.). Overall 4.68 vs 4.85 (n.s.) vs 5.34 (p=0.04). Excitement 4.55 vs 5.19 (p=0.04) vs 5.46.
limits: Reviewer-level and idea-level tests differ in significance for excitement and overall.
agent_relevance: Novelty alone is cheap to raise; the schema must pair novelty with a feasibility or effectiveness check.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Generated ideas were highly duplicated; the pool is far smaller than it looks.
numbers: From 4,000 generated seed ideas per topic, only about 200 (~5%) were non-duplicate at cosine similarity 0.8.
limits: Embedding threshold choice (0.8) is arbitrary; generation used one prompt pipeline.
agent_relevance: Sampling more from one model gives repeats, not breadth. Supports G4 (samples are not independent).

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Human experts agree only weakly on which ideas are good; LLM judges are near chance.
numbers: Inter-reviewer balanced accuracy 56.1% (NeurIPS 2021: 66.0%, ICLR 2024: 71.9%, random 50%). LLM judges vs human rankings: GPT-4o direct 50.0%, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0%, Claude-3.5 direct 51.7%, Claude-3.5 pairwise 53.3%, AI-Scientist reviewer 43.3%.
limits: Small judged set; labels are themselves noisy.
agent_relevance: Do not let the model grade novelty or promise. Use code-checked signals. Supports G5.

source: Si et al. (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap
finding: When experts actually executed the ideas (>100 hours each), LLM ideas lost their novelty and excitement advantage.
numbers: 19 human ideas, 24 AI ideas, 43 executors. Ideation novelty 4.912 human vs 5.778 AI (p=0.035); after execution 4.903 vs 4.729 (p=0.586). Score change AI: novelty -1.049, excitement -1.760, effectiveness -1.879, overall -1.976; human: -0.010, +0.078, -0.052, -0.628. Gap differences p=0.025, 0.001, 0.003, 0.004.
quote: the scores of the LLM-generated ideas decrease significantly more than expert-written ideas on all evaluation metrics
limits: Small N; short 4-page papers; NLP only; execution-stage differences between arms not significant, but ranking flipped on many metrics.
agent_relevance: Impact appears only after the work is done. A scaffold should test an idea by building and running it, not by rating it.

source: Si et al. (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap
finding: The paper did not test whether an LLM judge predicts execution outcomes; it notes prior work shows limits of LLM judges.
numbers: No LLM-judge-vs-outcome number in the paper.
limits: Absence of a test, not a negative result.
agent_relevance: Open question for our own measurement: does any cheap proxy predict executed-outcome value?

source: Gupta and Pruthi (2025) All That Glitters is Not Novel: Plagiarism in AI Generated Research
finding: Experts found a large share of LLM-generated 'novel' research proposals were copied or paraphrased from existing papers.
numbers: 50 documents, 13 experts. Verified by source-paper authors: 12/50 (24%) scored 4-5 (direct copy 5: 7; combined borrowing 4: 5). Unverified expert claims: 18/50 (36%). Only 2/50 (4%) rated fully original. Fresh proposals 7/36 plagiarised (19%); exemplars from Si et al. and AI Scientist papers 5/14 (36%).
limits: Authors call these a lower bound (rater time limits); human-paper comparison of 0.8%-6.3% was LLM-extracted from reviews, not comparable.
agent_relevance: Apparent novelty can be retrieval from memory. A novelty claim needs a literature search in code, not model opinion.

source: Gupta and Pruthi (2025) All That Glitters is Not Novel: Plagiarism in AI Generated Research
finding: Automated novelty and plagiarism checkers failed unless they were handed the source paper.
numbers: 480-paper synthetic set. Claude 3.5 Sonnet: oracle source 88.8%, parametric knowledge only 1.3%, retrieval pipeline (SSAG) 51.3%. GPT-4o: 89.0%, 32.7%, 68.5%. OpenScholar 0%, Turnitin 0% on 36 papers; OpenScholar found the true source in 1 real flagged case.
limits: Synthetic plagiarism made by GPT-4o rewriting; real cases are fewer.
agent_relevance: Retrieval, not judgment, is the bottleneck for any novelty check. Retrieval quality must be measured.

source: Gupta and Pruthi (2025) All That Glitters is Not Novel: Plagiarism in AI Generated Research
finding: LLM-generated proposals are more tightly clustered than human ones and easy to tell apart.
numbers: Cluster spread LLM/human 0.81 (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) and 0.72 (GPT-4o). Logistic regression on embeddings separates LLM from human proposals at 93.9% (Claude) and 92.6% (GPT-4o).
limits: Topic-controlled but one prompt pipeline.
agent_relevance: Homogeneity is a measurable property; a diversity count can run in code.

source: Gu and Krenn (2024) Generating Interesting Scientific Ideas using Knowledge Graphs and LLMs (SciMuse)
finding: Research-group leaders rated most personalised LLM ideas low; knowledge-graph selection did not help.
numbers: 4,451 ratings, 100+ leaders, 1-5 scale. Mean 2.403; 24.9% rated 4-5; most common rating 1 (36.7%). High-citation-predicted pairs 2.350, random pairs 2.446, titles-only GPT baseline 2.414.
limits: Personalised to each rater's own field; concept pairs only.
agent_relevance: Picking combinations by past impact did not raise rated interest. Selection by citation signals is not a free win.

source: Gu and Krenn (2024) Generating Interesting Scientific Ideas using Knowledge Graphs and LLMs (SciMuse)
finding: Predicted impact and expert interest moved in opposite directions on popularity features.
numbers: Interest fell as node degree, PageRank and citation counts rose, while predicted impact rose. High-citation-predicted pairs lower than random by 1.94 sigma (weak). Semantic distance lowered both interest and predicted impact.
limits: Weak evidence for the headline difference; no single correlation reported.
agent_relevance: Bears on Kaplan and Vakili style selection: popular combinations are not the interesting ones.

source: Gu and Krenn (2024) Generating Interesting Scientific Ideas using Knowledge Graphs and LLMs (SciMuse)
finding: Rated interest was only modestly predictable, and a zero-shot LLM ranker matched a trained network.
numbers: Neural net on graph features AUC 63.2%; GPT-4o zero-shot ranking AUC 67.4% (top-5 precision 45.8%), GPT-3.5 AUC 60.4%; net top-5 precision 49.2%.
limits: Targets are one person's rating; AUC near 0.65.
agent_relevance: A weak selector exists but is far from reliable. Use it to order, never to decide alone.

source: Predicting Empirical AI Research Outcomes with Language Models (2025)
finding: A fine-tuned model beat both experts and off-the-shelf models at predicting which of two AI research ideas would work empirically.
numbers: Test 1,585 post-cutoff pairs; train 6,000. Fine-tuned GPT-4.1 with retrieval 77.0% vs GPT-4.1 zero-shot 51.4%; GPT-3.5 zero-shot 45.0%. On 45 NLP pairs: fine-tuned 64.4%, 5-expert majority vote 48.9%, best-per-topic expert 60.0%. Unpublished AI-generated ideas: 63.6% (33 pairs).
limits: Outcome = benchmark result, not long-run impact; narrow to AI/NLP; 33-pair novel test is tiny.
agent_relevance: Outcome prediction can be learned from labelled results, but frontier models without training were near chance. Our agent cannot rely on its own taste.

source: Predicting Empirical AI Research Outcomes with Language Models (2025)
finding: Self-generated chain-of-thought did not help outcome prediction; whole-paper summaries did.
numbers: Fine-tuning on raw labels 77.0% vs random self-CoT 48.0% vs LM-selected CoT 47.8%. Retrieval with abstracts-only summaries 38.8% vs whole-paper summaries 53.0% (600-example subset).
limits: Single base model family.
agent_relevance: Reasoning text before verdict did not add accuracy here. Retrieval depth mattered more.

source: Predicting Empirical AI Research Outcomes with Language Models (2025)
finding: Robustness tests found no big reliance on surface features; slight length bias.
numbers: 289 LM-designed hypotheses: accuracy 81.3% when supported, 68.5% when unsupported; 34 flagged. Annotation: 25 researchers, majority agreement 75.1%, mislabel rate 11% to 2.5% after four rounds.
limits: Human stress-test values only in figures.
agent_relevance: Check length bias in any ranker we build (consistent with G5 length-normalising).

source: Liang et al. (2023) Can LLMs provide useful feedback on research papers?
finding: GPT-4 review comments overlapped with human reviewers about as much as humans overlap with each other.
numbers: Nature family 3,096 papers: 30.85% GPT-4 vs 28.58% human-human. ICLR 1,709 papers: 39.23% vs 35.25%. User study 308 researchers: 57.4% found it helpful; 82.4% said more useful than some human reviews.
limits: Overlap is on comments, not on judging breakthrough potential; larger for weaker papers.
agent_relevance: LLMs can give useful critique of what exists; this is not the same as picking rare high-impact work.

source: Doshi and Hauser (2024) Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content
finding: Showing writers AI story ideas raised rated novelty and usefulness of individual stories.
numbers: N=293 writers, 600 evaluators, conditions: no AI, 1 AI idea, up to 5 AI ideas. Novelty +5.4% (b=0.207, p=0.021) and +8.1% (b=0.311, p<0.001); usefulness +3.7% and +9.0%. Low-creativity writers (low DAT): novelty +6.3% and +10.7%, usefulness +5.5% and +11.5%.
limits: Short 8-sentence stories; Prolific US sample.
agent_relevance: Prompting with outside ideas lifts the weakest thinkers most; a model is closer to a low-DAT writer than to an expert.

source: Doshi and Hauser (2024) Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content
finding: AI-assisted stories were more alike each other, so collective novelty fell.
numbers: Stories 5.2% (b=4.29, p<0.001) and 5.0% (b=4.11) more similar to the shown AI idea (human-only mean 82.85). Similarity to the average of other stories in the condition: b=0.871 (1 idea) and b=0.718 (5 ideas), p<0.001 and p=0.003. 88.4% used AI at least once.
limits: Embedding cosine similarity measure.
agent_relevance: Individual gain with group-level loss is the same pattern as correlated samples in G4. Count diversity across attempts in code.

source: Wang, Downey, Ji, Hope (2023) SciMON: Scientific Inspiration Machines Optimized for Novelty
finding: SciMON retrieves inspirations and iteratively rewrites ideas against prior papers to raise novelty; the machine's ideas still fell short of real papers.
numbers: Iteration 1: 88.9% of updates substantially different; novelty raised for 55.6%. Iteration 2: raised for 57.8% of ideas that continued. Relative novelty improvement +54.4% (GPT4FS) to +55.6% (+SN). Ground-truth paper idea judged more technical and novel in 85% of comparisons.
quote: ideas are often based on superficial recombinations of common concepts
limits: Small annotated sets (about 5 annotators for the novelty study); novelty judged against related-work corpus.
agent_relevance: A working loop: generate, compare to retrieved prior work, rewrite only if too close. Fits G1 (revise on a signal). Depth stays low.

source: Wang, Downey, Ji, Hope (2023) SciMON: Scientific Inspiration Machines Optimized for Novelty
finding: Baseline GPT-4 ideas were rated low on technical depth and novelty; knowledge-graph context shifted pairwise preference.
numbers: GPT4FS+KG higher technical detail in 48% of pairs and less incremental in 45% of pairs; GPT4FS ranked higher than another baseline in 65% of cases in one study.
limits: Human-preference percentages, many ties.
agent_relevance: Retrieval context helps a little, not a lot.

source: Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models (2025)
finding: Different language models give strikingly similar answers to open-ended prompts, and one model repeats itself.
numbers: Infinity-Chat: 26K open-ended queries, 6 top-level and 17 sub categories, 31,250 human annotations, 25 annotators per example.
limits: Abstract page only read; per-model effect sizes not seen.
agent_relevance: Using several different models as 'diverse' voters gives less diversity than hoped. Supports G4.

source: Artificial Hivemind (2025)
finding: LLM judges and reward models are worse calibrated on items where humans disagree in taste.
numbers: Stated as a finding; no number on the abstract page.
limits: No numbers read.
agent_relevance: Rare high-impact work is exactly where human taste splits; model judges will mis-rank it.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery
finding: An agent pipeline generates ideas, runs experiments and writes papers, with an automated reviewer.
numbers: Under $15 per paper; three ML subfields; abstract says papers can exceed the acceptance threshold of a top ML conference.
limits: Abstract page only; no scores read. Gupta and Pruthi (c07) found 3 of its 10 exemplars scored 4-5 on plagiarism.
agent_relevance: Shows an LLM agent loop with a novelty-check step against literature search, but such checks proved weak (c08).

source: Li et al. (2024) Chain of Ideas: Revolutionizing Research via Novel Idea Development with LLM Agents
finding: Arranging literature as a chain showing how the field progressed was reported to improve idea generation; evaluated with an Idea Arena.
numbers: Cost about $0.50 per candidate idea with experiment design. No scores read.
limits: Abstract only; authors' own protocol.
agent_relevance: Chronological ordering of prior work is a cheap structure to try for novelty framing.

source: Nova (2024) An Iterative Planning and Search Approach to Enhance Novelty and Diversity of LLM Generated Ideas
finding: Planning retrieval of outside knowledge in rounds raised unique novel idea counts.
numbers: 3.4x as many unique novel ideas as the same system without it; at least 2.5x more top-rated ideas than prior state of the art; 170 seed papers, Swiss tournament.
limits: Abstract only; ratings by LLM and human, details unseen.
agent_relevance: Targeted retrieval beats resampling for breadth, consistent with c03.

source: Baek et al. (2024) ResearchAgent: Iterative Research Idea Generation over Scientific Literature with LLMs
finding: Agent builds on a core paper plus citation-graph neighbours and a concept store, with reviewer agents giving feedback over revision rounds.
numbers: No numbers on abstract page.
limits: Abstract only; authors claim 'novel, clear, and valid'.
agent_relevance: The reviewer-agent loop is the pattern G5 warns about (model judges); keep any critic blind to authorship.

source: AI Idea Bench 2025
finding: Benchmark of 3,495 AI papers scores generated ideas against the real paper they inspired; AI-Scientist led on alignment.
numbers: Idea-to-idea alignment motivation: AI-Scientist 3.591, VIRSCI 2.937, AI-Researcher 2.807, SCIPIP 2.437. Multiple-choice motivation: AI-Scientist 0.611, SCIPIP 0.595, AI-Researcher 0.566, VIRSCI 0.509.
limits: Page tables partly garbled; leakage of paper content into models is a stated concern.
agent_relevance: Ground-truth-from-later-paper benchmarks exist; pre-cutoff leakage must be controlled.

source: Kaplan and Vakili (2015) The double-edged sword of recombination in breakthrough innovation. Strategic Management Journal
finding: Not opened this session (publisher returned HTTP 403). Only the subfield row was read.
numbers: None verified.
limits: Unverified; do not cite figures from this line.
agent_relevance: Human-side anchor for the machine studies above. Needs a separate opened read.
